title: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
summary: Turn six scattered sensor readings into a map: nearest neighbor, inverse distance weighting, the semivariogram, ordinary kriging and its Gaussian process twin, and leave-one-out tests that decide which method to trust.
outcomes: Compute IDW weights and estimates for a target point and explain how the power p trades smoothness for locality
Build an empirical semivariogram from point pairs and fit a spherical model with nugget, sill and range
Set up and solve the ordinary kriging system, and interpret its weights, Lagrange multiplier and kriging variance
Explain why kriging is Gaussian process regression and map nugget, sill and mean assumptions to GP terms
Compare interpolators with leave-one-out RMSE and check kriging variance calibration with standardized errors

lessons.title: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging

blocks.md:
A city has six cheap PM2.5 sensors bolted to lamp posts. A dashboard wants a full map, and a resident at a location with no sensor wants to know the air quality right there. **Spatial interpolation** estimates a value at an unsampled location from values measured at scattered points.

The whole field rests on one assumption, stated by the geographer Waldo Tobler in a 1970 paper on urban growth in Detroit and now called *Tobler's first law of geography*: everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things. If readings were unrelated across space, no method could beat guessing the average.

Every method in this course is a **weighted average** of the readings:

- $\hat z(x_0) = \sum_i \lambda_i z_i$, where $x_0$ is the target location, $z_i$ is the reading at sensor $i$ and $\lambda_i$ is its weight.
- Methods differ only in how they choose the weights $\lambda_i$.

Nearest neighbor puts weight 1 on the closest sensor. Inverse distance weighting (IDW) uses distance alone. Kriging uses a fitted model of how similarity decays with distance, plus the geometry of the sensors relative to each other.

blocks.title: The toy: six sensors and one target (positions approximate)

scenes.caption: Six sensors on a 9 km by 7 km map, each reading PM2.5 in µg/m³. Coordinates are in km. S3 in the south-east reads 20, much higher than the rest. The grid layout is simplified; true coordinates are under each node.
The target is the point (4.5, 3), where no sensor exists. Every method will estimate it as a weighted average of the six readings.
Edge labels show the straight-line distance from each sensor to the target in km. S5 is closest (2.06 km), then S2 (2.50 km). S6 is farthest (4.61 km).
Nearest neighbor: all weight on S5, so the estimate is 16. One sensor decides everything, and the estimate jumps whenever the closest sensor changes.

blocks.md: Nearest neighbor turns the map into a patchwork of flat tiles, one per sensor. Each tile is a **Voronoi cell**: the set of locations closer to that sensor than to any other. The map below shows this on a 1 km grid. Values are discontinuous at tile borders, which is rarely true of air, temperature or elevation.

blocks.title: Nearest neighbor map on a 1 km grid (µg/m³)

scenes.caption: Rows are y from 7 (top) to 0, columns are x from 0 to 9. Each cell copies the reading of its nearest sensor, so the map is six flat tiles (Voronoi cells).
The S3 tile (reading 20) covers the whole south-east and then stops dead at its border with S2 and S5 tiles. A one-cell step changes the value from 16 or 11 to 20.

blocks.md:
Two smoother geometric methods are worth knowing. SciPy's [griddata](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.interpolate.griddata.html) with `method='linear'` tessellates the points into triangles (a Delaunay triangulation) and interpolates linearly inside each triangle. Our target sits inside the triangle S2, S3, S5 with barycentric weights 0.375, 0.125 and 0.5, giving 14.63. Outside the convex hull of the points it returns `fill_value` (NaN by default).

**Natural neighbor** interpolation, developed by Robin Sibson, inserts the target into the Voronoi diagram and weights each sensor by the share of the target's new cell that was taken from that sensor's old cell. Computed numerically for our target, the weights are S5 0.46, S2 0.31, S3 0.17, S1 0.04, S4 0.02 and S6 0, giving about 14.77.

Every interpolator here is a weighted average $\sum_i \lambda_i z_i$. The only question is how to pick the weights. Keep this frame: the rest of the course compares weight recipes on the same six sensors.

Interpolation is not the same as smoothing. Most of these methods are *exact*: the surface passes through every reading. That is right for precise instruments and wrong for noisy cheap sensors, where you want a method that can treat part of each reading as measurement error.

blocks.question: A colleague says nearest neighbor is safest because it never invents values that were not measured. What is the main weakness of the resulting map?
options: It cannot be computed without a fitted variogram
It is discontinuous: the value jumps at Voronoi cell borders even when the true field is smooth
It always returns the global mean far from sensors
It gives every sensor the same weight
blocks.explain: Nearest neighbor copies the closest reading, so the map is a set of flat Voronoi tiles with steps at the borders. It needs no model, and far from sensors it still copies the nearest one rather than the mean.

lessons.title: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone

blocks.md: In 1968 Donald Shepard, then an undergraduate working with the Harvard Laboratory for Computer Graphics on its SYMAP mapping program, published an interpolation function for irregularly spaced data that is now called **Shepard's method** or **inverse distance weighting (IDW)**. Each reading gets a weight that falls off as a power of its distance to the target, and the weights are normalized to sum to 1. GDAL's `gdal_grid` implements it as *inverse distance to a power*.

blocks.caption: $r_i$ is the distance from the target to sensor $i$ and $p > 0$ is the power. At a sensor location ($r_i = 0$) the method returns that sensor's reading.

blocks.md:
Work it for the target at (4.5, 3) with $p = 1$. The raw weights are $1/r_i$: S1 $1/3.64 = 0.275$, S2 $0.400$, S3 $0.312$, S4 $0.256$, S5 $0.485$, S6 $0.217$, summing to $1.945$. Dividing by the sum gives the normalized weights 0.141, 0.206, 0.161, 0.132, 0.249 and 0.112. The estimate is $0.141 \times 11 + 0.206 \times 11 + 0.161 \times 20 + 0.132 \times 9 + 0.249 \times 16 + 0.112 \times 11 = 13.43$.

With $p = 2$ the raw weights are $1/r_i^2$ and sum to $0.681$. Normalized: 0.111, 0.235, 0.143, 0.096, 0.346, 0.069. The estimate rises to 13.82 because S5 (reading 16) now holds 35% of the weight instead of 25%.

blocks.title: IDW weights at the target as the power p grows

scenes.caption: p = 1: weights fall off slowly with distance. Even S6, the farthest sensor, keeps 11%. Estimate 13.43.
p = 2 (the default power in gdal_grid): the closest sensors S5 and S2 now hold 58% of the weight together. Estimate 13.82.
p = 8: S5 holds 79% of the weight. Estimate 15.16. The surface starts to look like the nearest neighbor tiles.
p = 20: S5 holds 98% and the estimate is 15.90, almost the nearest neighbor answer of 16. As p grows, IDW turns into nearest neighbor.

blocks.title: How fast an IDW weight decays with distance

scenes.caption: Raw weight against distance for p = 1 and p = 2. The dots are our six sensors at their p = 2 raw weights. Only ratios matter, because the weights get normalized.
Drag p. At p = 4 the weight at 2.06 km (S5) is almost 6 times the weight at 3.2 km (S3); at p = 1 it is about 1.6 times. The power sets how local the average is.

blocks.md:
Two properties follow straight from the formula. First, all weights are positive and sum to 1, so an IDW estimate always lies between the smallest and largest reading: it can never predict a peak higher than any sensor saw. Second, for $p > 1$ the surface flattens out around every sensor, which creates the circular **bull's-eye** pattern typical of IDW maps.

A third is less obvious. In 2D, sensors at distance about $r$ grow in number like $r$, so the total weight of far sensors behaves like $\int r \cdot r^{-p}\,dr$. For $p \le 2$ that integral grows without bound as the area grows, so with many distant points the far field dominates. This is one reason implementations restrict IDW to a search radius or a maximum number of neighbors, like GDAL's search ellipse.

IDW ignores how sensors sit relative to each other. S1 and S2 are only 2.24 km apart and both read 11, so they carry nearly the same information. IDW still counts both at full weight. If ten sensors sat in one parking lot, IDW would let that lot outvote everything else. Kriging, later in the course, fixes this.

blocks.prompt: Without computing: if you set p very close to 0, what does the IDW estimate at the target approach?
blocks.reveal: Every weight $r_i^{-p}$ approaches 1, so all six sensors get weight $1/6$ and the estimate approaches the plain mean of the readings, $(11+11+20+9+16+11)/6 = 13.0$. So the power slides IDW between the global mean ($p \to 0$) and nearest neighbor ($p \to \infty$).

blocks.question: A monitoring network has a pollution source, and the true peak lies between sensors, higher than any sensor reading. Which statement about IDW is correct?
options: IDW with p = 2 will overshoot and predict a peak above all readings
IDW will predict the peak exactly if p is tuned by cross-validation
IDW always predicts the global mean between sensors
IDW cannot predict any value above the maximum reading, because its weights are positive and sum to 1
blocks.explain: An IDW estimate is a convex combination of the readings, so it lies between the minimum and maximum reading. No choice of p lets it exceed the highest sensor.

blocks.question: You switch an IDW map from p = 1 to p = 6. What happens to the map?
options: It approaches nearest neighbor: flat patches around each sensor with sharper transitions between them
It becomes smoother everywhere
It starts extrapolating trends beyond the readings
Nothing, because weights are normalized
blocks.explain: A large power makes the nearest sensor dominate, so the map looks like Voronoi tiles with steeper transitions. Normalization keeps weights summing to 1, but it does not undo the change in their ratios.

lessons.title: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance

blocks.md: IDW picks a power by habit. Kriging instead *measures* how similarity decays with distance in your data. The tool is the **semivariogram**: for two locations a distance $h$ apart, half the expected squared difference of their values. Small $\gamma(h)$ means points at that distance tend to read alike; large means they differ.

blocks.caption: Matheron's estimator, the default in scikit-gstat. $N(h)$ is the set of sensor pairs whose distance falls in the lag bin around $h$, and $\lvert N(h)\rvert$ in the denominator is its size.

blocks.md: Six sensors give $6 \times 5 / 2 = 15$ pairs. For each pair compute the distance and the semivariance $\frac{1}{2}(z_i - z_j)^2$. For example S2 (11) and S3 (20) are 4.00 km apart, so their semivariance is $\frac{1}{2} \times 9^2 = 40.5$. Then group pairs into distance bins (lags) and average within each bin. Here the bins are 0 to 3.5, 3.5 to 5, 5 to 6.5 and 6.5 to 8.5 km, each including its lower edge (so S1S5 at exactly 5.00 km goes in the third bin), chosen so every bin has at least 3 pairs.

blocks.title: All 15 sensor pairs, sorted by distance

scenes.caption: Each column is one pair of sensors: its distance and half its squared difference. Single pairs are noisy: S1S2 (2.24 km) has 0, while S4S5 (3.16 km) has 24.5.
Bin 1 (under 3.5 km, 3 pairs) and bin 2 (3.5 to 5 km, 4 pairs). Bin averages: (0 + 24.5 + 12.5) / 3 = 12.33 and (40.5 + 2 + 12.5 + 8) / 4 = 15.75.
Bin 3 (5 to 6.5 km, 5 pairs) averages 19.5 and bin 4 (6.5 to 8.5 km, 3 pairs) averages 20.17. Semivariance rises with distance, then levels off.
The largest values all involve S3 (reading 20): S3S4 60.5, S2S3, S3S6 and S1S3 40.5 each. One unusual sensor shapes the whole empirical variogram when there are only 15 pairs.

blocks.md:
The binned values are the **empirical variogram**. To use it for kriging we fit a smooth **variogram model** from a family known to be valid (one that always yields a non-negative variance for any weighted combination of points). Three parameters describe the common bounded models:

- **Nugget** $c_0$: the jump at distance near zero, from measurement error or variation at scales shorter than the closest pair.
- **Sill** $c_0 + c$: the plateau, the variance between points that are effectively unrelated. $c$ is the *partial sill*.
- **Range** $a$: the distance where the plateau is reached. Beyond it, readings are uncorrelated.

blocks.tex: \gamma(h)=\begin{cases} c_0 + c\left(\dfrac{3h}{2a}-\dfrac{h^3}{2a^3}\right) & 0 < h \le a\\ c_0 + c & h > a\end{cases}
blocks.caption: The spherical model, as defined in the PyKrige docs (with $p$ = partial sill $c$, $r$ = range $a$, $n$ = nugget $c_0$). It reaches the sill exactly at the range.

blocks.title: Fitting a spherical model to the four bins

scenes.caption: A poor first guess: range 3 km, sill 15. The curve plateaus too early and too low; bins 3 and 4 sit well above it.
Weighted least squares (each bin weighted by its pair count, nugget fixed at 0) gives partial sill 20.3 and range 6.9 km. Model values at the bins: 11.87, 16.43, 19.06, 20.30.
Letting the nugget float gives nugget 0.68, partial sill 19.68, range 7.0 km: nearly the same curve. With 15 pairs, the data cannot tell these apart.
An exponential model with the same numbers rises faster at short lags and only approaches the sill. In PyKrige its range parameter is a practical range, where about 95% of the sill is reached.

blocks.md: Library defaults differ, so read them. PyKrige's `OrdinaryKriging` defaults to a *linear* variogram model with `nlags=6` and fits parameters automatically if you do not pass them. scikit-gstat's `Variogram` defaults to the Matheron estimator, a spherical model, `n_lags=10` evenly spaced bins and a trust-region least squares fit (`fit_method='trf'`). Both support spherical, exponential and Gaussian models among others.

An empirical variogram from a handful of points is very noisy, and the fitted range and nugget can swing a lot with the bin edges or the fitting weights. Look at the plot, try a second binning and treat the parameters as uncertain, not as measured truths.
The variogram turns Tobler's law into numbers: how much readings disagree, on average, as a function of distance. Its nugget, sill and range are what kriging uses to decide weights.

blocks.question: Your fitted variogram has a large nugget, almost equal to the sill. What does this say about your sensors?
options: Readings are strongly correlated at all distances, so interpolation will be very accurate
The range must be zero, so kriging cannot be run
Even very close sensors disagree about as much as distant ones, so spatial interpolation adds little over the mean
Close sensors always agree exactly
blocks.explain: The nugget is the semivariance as distance approaches zero. If it is almost the sill, nearby pairs differ about as much as unrelated pairs: the measurable spatial structure is weak (or dominated by measurement error), and kriging estimates approach the mean.

blocks.question: Why fit a model like the spherical one instead of plugging the four empirical bin values directly into kriging?
options: The empirical values are in the wrong units
Kriging needs semivariance at arbitrary distances, and the model must be a valid one so that every predicted variance is non-negative
Spherical models always fit better than the empirical values
Fitting removes the need to choose a nugget
blocks.explain: Kriging asks for $\gamma$ at every sensor-to-sensor and sensor-to-target distance, not just the bin centers, and arbitrary numbers can produce negative variances. Valid model families avoid that.

lessons.title: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights

blocks.md:
**Ordinary kriging** asks: of all weighted averages $\hat z(x_0) = \sum_i \lambda_i z_i$, which one has the smallest expected squared error, under the variogram model? It assumes the field has a constant but *unknown* mean in the neighborhood. Requiring the weights to sum to 1 makes the estimate unbiased whatever that mean is. GSTools describes this exactly: with the unbiased option the weights must sum to 1, giving ordinary kriging; without it you get simple kriging, where the mean must be given.

Minimizing the error variance subject to $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$ with a Lagrange multiplier $\mu$ (an extra unknown that enforces the constraint) gives a linear system with one row per sensor plus one constraint row.

blocks.caption: $\Gamma_{ij} = \gamma(\lVert s_i - s_j \rVert)$ between sensors, $(\boldsymbol\gamma_0)_i = \gamma(\lVert s_i - x_0 \rVert)$ from each sensor to the target. The kriging variance formula is the one the scikit-gstat guide uses.

blocks.title: The 7 by 7 ordinary kriging matrix (spherical, sill 20.3, range 6.9)

scenes.caption: Top-left 6 by 6 block: model semivariance between every pair of sensors. Zeros on the diagonal (no nugget). Pairs at least 6.9 km apart, like S1 and S6, get the full sill 20.3.
S1 and S2 are only 2.24 km apart, so $\gamma$ between them is small (9.52). The system sees that they are redundant, which IDW never does.
The last row and column of ones enforce $\sum \lambda_i = 1$; the extra unknown is the Lagrange multiplier $\mu$. Solving gives the weights and $\mu = -0.242$.

blocks.title: Right-hand side and solution for the target (4.5, 3)

scenes.caption: $\gamma_0$: model semivariance from each sensor to the target. S5 is closest, so its value is smallest (8.83). Smaller semivariance means more similar to the target.
Solved OK weights. S5 gets 0.477 and S2 0.322, more concentrated than IDW p = 2 (0.346 and 0.235). The weights sum to exactly 1.
Declustering: S1 is about as far from the target as S3, but sits next to S2. OK gives S1 only 0.042 (IDW p = 2 gave 0.111) because S2 already carries that information.
Screening: S6 lies farther out on the same side as S5, which sits between it and the target, so OK gives it a negative weight, -0.056. IDW weights can never be negative.

blocks.md:
Plug in: $\hat z = 0.042 \times 11 + 0.322 \times 11 + 0.195 \times 20 + 0.020 \times 9 + 0.477 \times 16 - 0.056 \times 11 = 15.10$. The kriging variance is $\boldsymbol\lambda^\top \boldsymbol\gamma_0 + \mu = 10.12 - 0.24 = 9.88$, a standard deviation of 3.14 µg/m³. Under a Gaussian assumption that is a rough 95% interval of 8.9 to 21.3. PyKrige's `OrdinaryKriging` with the same spherical parameters returns 15.0986 and 9.8754 at this point, matching the numpy solve.

Compare: nearest neighbor 16, IDW 13.43 ($p = 1$) and 13.82 ($p = 2$), linear triangulation 14.63, natural neighbor about 14.77, ordinary kriging 15.10.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
P = np.array([[1,2],[3,1],[7,1],[2,6],[5,5],[8,6]], float)
z = np.array([11, 11, 20, 9, 16, 11], float)
x0 = np.array([4.5, 3.0])

def sph(h, c0=0.0, c=20.3, a=6.9):
    r = np.minimum(h / a, 1.0)
    return np.where(h > 0, c0 + c * (1.5 * r - 0.5 * r**3), 0.0)

n = len(z)
A = np.ones((n + 1, n + 1)); A[n, n] = 0.0
A[:n, :n] = sph(np.linalg.norm(P[:, None] - P[None], axis=2))
g0 = sph(np.linalg.norm(P - x0, axis=1))
sol = np.linalg.solve(A, np.r_[g0, 1.0])
lam, mu = sol[:n], sol[n]
print(lam.round(3), lam @ z, lam @ g0 + mu)  # weights, 15.10, 9.88
blocks.caption: Ordinary kriging for one target in a dozen lines of numpy.

scenes.caption: Kriging variance on the 1 km grid. It is exactly 0 at the six sensor cells, because ordinary kriging without a nugget is an exact interpolator.
Variance is largest at the map corners, far from every sensor: 15.8 at (0, 7) and 15.9 at (9, 0). There the estimate is little better than the mean, and the map says so.

blocks.prompt: Suppose every sensor reading doubled but the locations and the variogram model stayed the same. What happens to the kriging variance map?
blocks.reveal: Nothing. The kriging weights and variance depend only on the variogram model and the geometry of sensors and target; the readings $z_i$ never enter $\Gamma$ or $\boldsymbol\gamma_0$. The readings affect the variance only indirectly, through the variogram you fit from them. So kriging variance tells you where your *network* is thin, not where the field is hard to predict.

blocks.md: Kriging weights come from solving a linear system, not from a fixed formula. That lets them account for redundancy between sensors (declustering) and for sensors hidden behind others (screening), and it yields an error variance for every estimate.

Negative weights mean an ordinary kriging estimate can fall outside the range of the readings. That can be right for a smooth field with a peak between sensors, but for quantities that must stay positive (rainfall, concentrations) check for negative predictions.

blocks.question: The ordinary kriging system has an extra row of ones and an extra unknown $\mu$. What would go wrong if you dropped them and just solved $\Gamma \boldsymbol\lambda = \boldsymbol\gamma_0$?
options: The weights would no longer be forced to sum to 1, so the estimate would be biased whenever the unknown mean is not zero
Nothing; the row only speeds up the solve
The estimate would ignore the nearest sensor
The matrix would become 8 by 8
blocks.explain: The constraint row enforces $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$, which makes the estimate unbiased for any constant mean. Without it the weights can sum to anything, and the estimate is pulled toward or away from zero.

blocks.question: Two sensors sit 10 m apart and read 30 and 31. A third sensor equally far from the target, in another direction, reads 12. Compared with IDW, how will ordinary kriging weight them (assume a range of several km)?
options: Exactly like IDW, because the distances to the target are equal
It gives the pair all the weight because they agree with each other
It gives every sensor weight 1/3 regardless of position
It gives the close pair less weight each, treating them almost like one sensor, and the lone sensor relatively more
blocks.explain: The pair is nearly redundant: $\Gamma$ shows they are strongly correlated with each other, so kriging splits roughly one sensor's worth of weight between them. IDW only looks at distance to the target, so it counts the pair twice.

lessons.title: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates

blocks.md:
Kriging comes from mining geostatistics: Georges Matheron named the method after the South African mining engineer D. G. Krige. Rasmussen and Williams note in *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning* (section 2.8) that Gaussian process prediction is well known in geostatistics, where it is known as kriging. GSTools says the same in its docs: its `krige` module provides routines for Gaussian process regression, also known as kriging.

A Gaussian process (GP) models the unknown field as random values at every location, any finite set of which is jointly Gaussian with a chosen mean and covariance function (kernel); GP regression predicts by conditioning on the readings. The bridge is the covariance. For a stationary field with a bounded variogram, the covariance at distance $h$ is $C(h) = C(0) - \gamma(h)$, where $C(0)$ is the sill. Our spherical model gives $C(0) = 20.3$ and $C(h) = 0$ beyond 6.9 km.

blocks.caption: GPML equations 2.25 and 2.26: the GP posterior mean and variance with zero prior mean. $K$ is the sensor covariance matrix, $\mathbf{k}_*$ the covariances to the target, $\sigma_n^2$ the noise variance.

blocks.md:
Map the pieces:

- **Simple kriging** is the zero-mean GP posterior applied to $z - m$ with a *known* mean $m$. With $m$ = the sample mean 13.0 and no noise, the weights are 0.049, 0.326, 0.204, 0.029, 0.479 and -0.046. They sum to 1.042, not 1, and the estimate is 15.090 with variance 9.865.
- **Ordinary kriging** treats the mean as unknown. GPML section 2.7 adds explicit basis functions $h(x)$ with a Gaussian prior on their coefficients; with $h(x) = 1$ and a vague prior (eq. 2.42), the posterior mean and variance at our target are 15.099 and 9.875, identical to the ordinary kriging solve. The implied mean (a generalized least squares estimate) is 12.80.
- The **nugget** plays the role of the noise term $\sigma_n^2$ on the diagonal: it is why PyKrige's and GSTools' non-exact modes stop forcing the surface through every reading.

scenes.caption: Geostatistics speaks in variograms, machine learning in covariance functions (kernels). For a stationary field with a sill they carry the same information.
Simple kriging with a known mean equals the GP posterior mean of GPML eq. 2.25 applied to the residuals from that mean.
Ordinary kriging equals a GP with a constant mean function under a vague prior (GPML eq. 2.42). On our toy both give 15.099 with variance 9.875.
A nugget is a noise term on the diagonal. With it, the posterior mean no longer passes exactly through the readings, which is what you want for noisy sensors.

blocks.md: What each side brings. Geostatistics brings variogram diagnostics, anisotropy, block kriging and decades of practice with 2D and 3D fields. The GP view brings marginal likelihood for fitting kernel parameters, many kernels (Matern, periodic, sums of kernels), extra input features beyond coordinates, and scalable approximations. SciPy's `RBFInterpolator` is a close cousin: it also solves a linear system for kernel coefficients plus a low-degree polynomial, with a `smoothing` term that plays the nugget's role, but it has no probabilistic variance.

Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

blocks.question: Two estimates at the same point: simple kriging with an assumed mean of 13.0 gives 15.090; ordinary kriging gives 15.099. Why do they differ slightly?
options: Ordinary kriging uses a different variogram
Simple kriging ignores the nearest sensor
Simple kriging's weights need not sum to 1, so the assumed mean gets weight 1 minus their sum; ordinary kriging estimates the mean from the data instead
They are numerically unstable; the difference is rounding error
blocks.explain: Simple kriging writes the estimate as $m + \sum \lambda_i (z_i - m)$, so the known mean carries the leftover weight (here $1 - 1.042$). Ordinary kriging forces the weights to sum to 1, which is equivalent to using a data-estimated mean (12.80 here).

blocks.question: A data scientist fits a GP to sensor data with an RBF kernel plus a white noise kernel. In kriging vocabulary, the white noise variance corresponds to:
options: The range
The sill
The nugget
The Lagrange multiplier
blocks.explain: A white noise term adds variance only on the diagonal, exactly like a nugget: semivariance jumps from 0 to the nugget as soon as two points are distinct.

lessons.title: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation

blocks.md: Which interpolator should the dashboard use? Do not trust the theory alone: kriging is optimal *if* its variogram model is right, which on six sensors is a big if. Measure instead with **leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO)**: hide one sensor, predict its reading from the other five, record the error, repeat for every sensor, and summarize with root mean squared error (RMSE).

blocks.title: Leave-one-out over six sensors

scenes.caption: For each method, loop over the six sensors. Fold i hides sensor i and keeps the other five.
Fold 0: ordinary kriging predicts 10.24 at S1 from the other five; the truth is 11, so the error is -0.76.
Fold 2 hides S3 (reading 20). No remaining sensor is close to it or reads high, so kriging predicts 11.73, an error of -8.27. Every method misses this fold badly.

blocks.prompt: Predict the ranking by LOO RMSE on these six sensors: global mean of the other five, nearest neighbor, IDW p = 1, IDW p = 2 and ordinary kriging.
blocks.reveal: Kriging does **not** win. RMSE: IDW p = 1 4.51, the plain mean 4.54, IDW p = 2 4.55, ordinary kriging 5.05 and nearest neighbor 5.83. With five points per fold, no method meaningfully beats the mean (only IDW p = 1 edges past it; the rest are worse), and the S3 fold alone is 45% to 57% of each method's squared error (40% for nearest neighbor). A variogram fitted to 15 pairs is a weak model, and LOO exposes that.

blocks.title: Leave-one-out RMSE on the six sensors (µg/m³)

scenes.caption: Baseline: predict each hidden sensor with the mean of the other five. RMSE 4.54. Any useful interpolator must beat this.
Nearest neighbor is worst at 5.83: hiding S5 makes it copy S4 (9) for a true 16, and hiding S4 makes it copy S5.
IDW p = 1 scores 4.51 and p = 2 scores 4.55: no better than the mean in practice. Ordinary kriging scores 5.05.

Dropping the S3 fold changes the picture: RMSE over the other five folds is 3.26 for the mean, 3.35 for IDW p = 1, 3.50 for IDW p = 2, 4.11 for kriging and 4.96 for nearest neighbor. One fold dominates six-fold LOO.

blocks.md:
Kriging also predicts its own error, so LOO can check that too. Divide each error by the kriging standard deviation for that fold. If the variances are calibrated, the mean of these squared standardized errors should be near 1. Here it is 1.32: the errors are larger than the kriging variance claims, mostly because of S3 (standardized error -1.76).

Two honest caveats. The variogram was fitted once on all six sensors, so each fold's model has seen the hidden reading; a strict LOO would refit the variogram inside every fold. And six folds give a very noisy RMSE: the ranking could flip with one more sensor.

blocks.title: Four maps of the same six readings (µg/m³)

scenes.caption: Nearest neighbor: flat Voronoi tiles with hard edges.
IDW p = 1: very smooth, pulled toward the overall mean almost everywhere, with small spikes at each sensor.
IDW p = 2: visible bull's-eyes around S3 (20) and S5 (16), flattening between sensors.
Ordinary kriging: a broad high region from S3 toward S5 and smooth decay elsewhere. It honors every reading exactly, like IDW, but its shape follows the fitted variogram.

blocks.md:
Practical guidance that follows from all of this:

- **Start with a baseline** (mean, nearest neighbor) and cross-validate every candidate on the same folds.
- **IDW** is fast, needs no model and is a reasonable baseline; tune $p$ and the search radius by cross-validation.
- **Kriging** pays off when the variogram is well estimated, when sensors cluster, and when you need an uncertainty map. Use a nugget for noisy sensors.
- **Cost**: a global kriging or RBF solve is a dense $n \times n$ system. SciPy notes that `RBFInterpolator` memory grows quadratically and becomes impractical beyond about a thousand points without its `neighbors` option; scikit-gstat's `OrdinaryKriging` similarly takes `min_points` and `max_points` to krige from local neighborhoods.

Kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor only under its own model. With few points, an unreliable variogram can make it worse than IDW, as in this toy. Its variance map is only as trustworthy as the variogram, so check calibration with standardized LOO errors.

Choose interpolators by held-out error, not by reputation. Leave-one-out RMSE (or blocked cross-validation) compares methods on your data, and the standardized errors tell you whether kriging's uncertainty can be trusted.

blocks.question: Ordinary kriging's leave-one-out standardized errors have a mean square of 3.0 on a large network. What is the most likely problem?
options: The kriging variances are too small, for example because the nugget or sill is underestimated
The estimates are biased because the weights do not sum to 1
IDW would have exactly the same issue, so it does not matter
The kriging variances are too large, so the model is too cautious
blocks.explain: Squared standardized errors averaging well above 1 mean actual errors are larger than the predicted standard deviations, so the model is overconfident. Underestimating the nugget (treating noisy readings as exact) or the sill is a common cause.

blocks.question: You have 5,000 weather stations and need a 1 km map nightly. Global ordinary kriging is too slow. Which change keeps most of kriging's benefits?
options: Switch to nearest neighbor
Krige from a local neighborhood of the nearest few dozen stations per target, using a variogram fitted once on all stations
Drop the variogram and set all weights to 1/5000
Use IDW with p = 0
blocks.explain: Local neighborhoods (like scikit-gstat's max_points or RBFInterpolator's neighbors) make each solve small. Distant stations get negligible weight beyond the range anyway, so the map changes little while cost drops sharply.
